newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope will spend 25 hours in Sarajevo next month.
newsitem.headline: Pope will spend 25 hours in Sarajevo next month.

text.p: Pope John Paul will spend 25 hours in Sarajevo next month on a delicate trip to the Bosnian capital that has raised fears for his safety.
The highlights of the April 12-13 trip will be a mass in Kosevo stadium and a meeting with non-Catholic religious leaders, according to a Vatican programme issued on Tuesday.
The main aim of the trip, his first abroad this year, is to preach religious reconciliation to a land torn apart by four years of inter-communal war underscored by religious divisions.
The Pope had to cancel a trip to Sarajevo at the last minute in September 1994 because of security fears.
The 76-year-old Polish Pontiff arrives in Sarajevo on the afternoon of Saturday, April 12 and will deliver eight homilies and addresses before returning to Rome on Sunday afternoon.

Fears for the the Pope's safety have been sparked by a spate of recent attacks on Roman Catholic churches in Bosnia's Croat-Moslem federation, including an explosion earlier this month in a downtown Sarajevo church.
The Catholic Church information office for the Papal visit was quoted in Bosnian newspapers as saying it had received threatening phone calls and had to shut for a day.

Religion underlies the conflict which has torn apart Bosnia, a united region under former Yugoslavia, now largely divided into separate communities of Orthodox Serbs, Roman Catholic Croats and Moslems.
The Croatian government has called on Bosnian Moslem authorities to take forceful action to stop attacks on Roman Catholic property prior to the trip.
Bosnian Moslem authorities had pledged to step up security around Catholic churches and buildings before this month's bombing.
Tension has been running high in the federation since Croat police opened fire on Moslems trying to visit a cemetery in Croat-held western Mostar last month.
The Moslem-Croat war ended with a U.S-brokered federation agreement in March 1994, but power-sharing and efforts to allow refugees to return home have run into obstacles on both sides.
